title: Audit Evidence - Sufficiency and Appropriateness
exam_relevance: CRITICAL - Heavily tested on CPA AUD exam. Expect 5-8 questions on evidence concepts, reliability hierarchy, and evidence types. Understanding evidence sufficiency and appropriateness is fundamental to all audit questions.
learning_objectives: Understand the dual nature of audit evidence: sufficiency (quantity) and appropriateness (quality)
Master the hierarchy of evidence reliability and know which evidence is most persuasive
Identify and apply the seven primary types of audit evidence and their characteristics
Evaluate evidence reliability based on source, nature, and circumstances
Understand how to respond when evidence is contradictory or insufficient
Apply professional skepticism in evidence evaluation
Link evidence-gathering procedures to financial statement assertions
Understand the relationship between evidence, audit risk, and materiality

introduction.overview: Audit evidence comprises all the information used by the auditor in arriving at the conclusions on which the audit opinion is based. The auditor's objective is to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to reduce audit risk to an acceptably low level and thereby enable the auditor to draw reasonable conclusions on which to base the audit opinion.
introduction.key_standard: AU-C Section 500 (Audit Evidence) provides the primary guidance on evidence requirements. This standard emphasizes that the auditor must design and perform audit procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence.
introduction.fundamental_concept: Evidence has TWO critical dimensions that must both be satisfied: SUFFICIENCY (quantity - how much evidence) and APPROPRIATENESS (quality - how reliable and relevant the evidence is). More evidence does not compensate for poor quality, and high quality does not eliminate the need for adequate quantity.

sufficiency_vs_appropriateness.description: The two dimensions of audit evidence work together - the auditor needs BOTH sufficient AND appropriate evidence.

sufficiency.definition: Sufficiency is the measure of the QUANTITY of audit evidence. The auditor needs enough evidence to support their conclusions.

factors_affecting_sufficiency.risk_of_material_misstatement: Higher risk requires MORE evidence. If management has incentive to overstate revenue, you need more evidence about revenue.
factors_affecting_sufficiency.quality_of_evidence: Lower quality evidence requires MORE quantity to compensate. If you can't confirm receivables, you need more alternative procedures.
factors_affecting_sufficiency.size_of_population: Larger populations generally require larger sample sizes.
factors_affecting_sufficiency.audit_experience: Prior experience with the client may affect the amount of evidence needed, but cannot eliminate the need for current-year evidence.
factors_affecting_sufficiency.materiality: More material items require more evidence. A $10 million receivable needs more testing than a $1,000 receivable.

sufficiency.professional_judgment: There's no formula for 'enough' evidence - it requires professional judgment based on the circumstances. The auditor must use experience and consider the specific risks present.

appropriateness.definition: Appropriateness is the measure of the QUALITY of audit evidence - both its relevance and its reliability.

relevance.description: Evidence is relevant when it has a logical relationship to the assertion being tested.
relevance.example_1: Testing inventory observation is RELEVANT to the existence assertion for inventory.
relevance.example_2: Testing customer confirmations is RELEVANT to the existence assertion for accounts receivable.
relevance.example_3: Examining vendor invoices is RELEVANT to the valuation assertion for purchases.
relevance.not_relevant_example: Testing the existence of equipment would NOT be relevant to testing the completeness of accounts payable.
relevance.key_point: Evidence can be highly reliable but irrelevant to the assertion being tested - it would not be appropriate audit evidence for that purpose.

reliability.description: Reliability refers to how dependable and trustworthy the evidence is. More reliable evidence is more persuasive.
reliability.hierarchy_overview: There is a clear hierarchy of evidence reliability that auditors must understand and apply when designing procedures.
reliability.importance: CPA exam questions frequently test whether candidates can identify which evidence is MORE reliable in different situations.

sufficiency_vs_appropriateness.relationship: Sufficiency and appropriateness are interrelated. If evidence quality is lower (less appropriate), the auditor needs more of it (greater sufficiency). However, obtaining more evidence cannot fully compensate for poor quality. For example, 100 unconfirmed customer balances are less persuasive than 50 confirmed balances.

evidence_reliability_hierarchy.description: AU-C 500 provides clear guidance on factors that affect the reliability of audit evidence. Understanding this hierarchy is CRITICAL for the CPA exam.
evidence_reliability_hierarchy.exam_importance: Expect multiple questions asking you to identify which evidence is MORE reliable or MOST persuasive. Memorize this hierarchy.

factor_1_source_external_vs_internal.rule: Evidence obtained from INDEPENDENT SOURCES OUTSIDE the entity is MORE reliable than evidence obtained from internal sources.
factor_1_source_external_vs_internal.rationale: External parties are independent and have no reason to misstate information to benefit the client.

more_reliable: Bank confirmation obtained directly from the bank
Customer confirmation of accounts receivable balance
Vendor statements received directly from vendors
Property tax assessment from county records
less_reliable: Company's internal accounts receivable aging report

factor_1_source_external_vs_internal.exam_tip: When a question asks which procedure provides the MOST reliable evidence, external evidence almost always wins over internal evidence.

factor_2_auditor_generated.rule: Evidence generated by the AUDITOR is MORE reliable than evidence provided by the entity.
factor_2_auditor_generated.rationale: When the auditor performs the procedure directly, there's no risk of client manipulation.

more_reliable_auditor_generated: Auditor's physical observation of inventory count

factor_2_auditor_generated.key_distinction: REPERFORMANCE (auditor does it) is more reliable than INSPECTION (auditor looks at what client did).

factor_3_internal_controls.rule: Evidence obtained when internal controls are EFFECTIVE is MORE reliable than evidence obtained when controls are weak or ineffective.
factor_3_internal_controls.rationale: Strong controls reduce the risk that information is misstated, making evidence from the client's system more trustworthy.

examples.strong_controls_scenario: If the client has excellent IT general controls, segregation of duties, and robust reconciliation processes, the auditor can place more reliance on system-generated reports.
examples.weak_controls_scenario: If the client has poor controls, lacks segregation of duties, and has control deficiencies, the auditor must obtain more evidence from external sources or perform more substantive testing.
examples.impact_on_testing: Effective controls allow the auditor to reduce substantive testing. Weak controls require more extensive substantive procedures.

factor_3_internal_controls.exam_application: If a question describes weak controls, you should select procedures that gather MORE external evidence or MORE auditor-generated evidence.

factor_4_direct_knowledge.rule: Evidence obtained DIRECTLY by the auditor is MORE reliable than evidence obtained INDIRECTLY or by inference.

direct_evidence: Auditor obtains confirmation directly from customer
Auditor inspects equipment at client site
indirect_evidence: Auditor reviews photos of inventory taken by client
Auditor reviews confirmation returned to client (not sent directly to auditor)
Auditor reviews maintenance records instead of inspecting equipment
Auditor reviews petty cash reimbursement vouchers

factor_4_direct_knowledge.confirmation_example: A confirmation sent directly to the auditor at the auditor's address is MORE reliable than one returned to the client's address (risk of interception).

factor_5_documentary_form.rule: Evidence in DOCUMENTARY form (paper or electronic) is MORE reliable than ORAL representations.
factor_5_documentary_form.rationale: Written evidence creates a record that can be examined, verified, and doesn't rely on memory. Oral evidence can be forgotten, misremembered, or later denied.

oral_less_reliable: Verbal discussion with management about inventory obsolescence
Conversation with purchasing manager about vendors

factor_5_documentary_form.exam_note: Management representations are REQUIRED but are the LEAST reliable form of evidence. They must be corroborated with other procedures.

factor_6_original_documents.rule: ORIGINAL documents are MORE reliable than PHOTOCOPIES or FACSIMILES.
factor_6_original_documents.rationale: Original documents are harder to alter. Photocopies can be manipulated before copying.
factor_6_original_documents.modern_context: In today's digital environment, electronically generated documents are considered originals if they come from secure, controlled systems.

examples.more_reliable: Original vendor invoice with shipping documents
examples.less_reliable: Photocopy of vendor invoice provided by accounts payable clerk

factor_6_original_documents.exam_relevance: Less frequently tested today given electronic records, but still appears occasionally in questions about document examination.

reliability_ranking_summary.description: When evaluating evidence, apply this ranking from MOST to LEAST reliable:
ranking: 1. MOST RELIABLE: External evidence obtained directly by auditor from independent sources (e.g., confirmation sent directly to auditor)
2. HIGHLY RELIABLE: Evidence generated directly by auditor (e.g., auditor's physical observation, recalculation)
3. RELIABLE: External evidence obtained by client when controls are strong (e.g., vendor statements when controls are effective)
4. MODERATELY RELIABLE: Internal evidence when controls are strong (e.g., system-generated reports with effective IT controls)
5. LESS RELIABLE: Internal evidence when controls are weak
6. LEAST RELIABLE: Management representations and oral explanations
reliability_ranking_summary.exam_strategy: When asked which procedure provides the MOST persuasive evidence, select the option that ranks highest in this hierarchy.

types_of_audit_evidence.description: AU-C 500 identifies seven primary types of audit procedures for obtaining audit evidence. Each type has different characteristics and provides different levels of reliability.
types_of_audit_evidence.exam_importance: You must know all seven types, be able to identify them in scenarios, and understand which assertions they best address.

type_1_inspection_of_records_and_documen.definition: Examining records or documents, whether internal or external, in paper form, electronic form, or other media.
type_1_inspection_of_records_and_documen.reliability: Varies based on source and nature. External documents are more reliable than internal. Original documents more reliable than copies.
examples: Examining vendor invoices to verify purchases
Inspecting sales invoices and shipping documents for revenue recognition
Reviewing contracts to understand terms and obligations
Examining canceled checks for cash disbursements
Inspecting title documents for property ownership
Reviewing bank statements
Examining lease agreements
Inspecting loan agreements and debt covenants

assertions_tested.occurrence_existence: Invoices and shipping documents provide evidence that transactions occurred
assertions_tested.rights_and_obligations: Contracts and title documents evidence ownership
assertions_tested.valuation: Vendor invoices support valuation of purchases
assertions_tested.completeness: More difficult - inspection usually doesn't prove completeness (can't see what's missing)

type_1_inspection_of_records_and_documen.strengths: Provides detailed, specific evidence about transactions and balances
type_1_inspection_of_records_and_documen.limitations: Documents can be forged or altered. Inspection doesn't prove completeness.
type_1_inspection_of_records_and_documen.exam_tip: Inspection of EXTERNALLY created documents (vendor invoices, bank statements) is more reliable than INTERNALLY created documents (company-prepared schedules).

type_2_inspection_of_tangible_assets.definition: Physical examination of assets. Provides reliable evidence about physical existence but may not address valuation, rights, or obligations.
type_2_inspection_of_tangible_assets.reliability: HIGH for existence, LOWER for valuation and rights
examples: Observing inventory counts
Inspecting fixed assets (equipment, buildings, vehicles)
Counting petty cash
Examining securities held as investments
Inspecting construction work in progress

assertions_tested.existence: STRONGEST - physical inspection directly confirms asset exists
assertions_tested.valuation: WEAK - seeing inventory doesn't tell you its market value or whether it's obsolete
assertions_tested.rights_and_obligations: WEAK - observing equipment doesn't prove the company owns it (could be leased)
assertions_tested.completeness: WEAK - you can count what's there but can't see what's missing

limitations.valuation_issue: You can see that equipment exists, but inspection doesn't tell you its fair value or whether it's impaired
limitations.ownership_issue: Physical possession doesn't prove ownership - need to inspect title documents
limitations.completeness_issue: Can't identify assets that should be recorded but aren't physically present

type_2_inspection_of_tangible_assets.exam_scenario: Questions often ask: 'The auditor observed inventory. Which assertion is addressed?' Answer: EXISTENCE, not valuation or rights.
type_2_inspection_of_tangible_assets.best_used_for: Existence assertion for tangible assets, particularly inventory and fixed assets

type_3_observation.definition: Watching a process or procedure being performed by others. Provides evidence about how procedures are performed at a point in time.
type_3_observation.reliability: MODERATE - evidence is only about that specific point in time. Observation may influence the process (people may perform better when being watched).
examples: Observing the client's physical inventory count procedures
Watching the opening of incoming mail to assess cash receipts controls
Observing the IT access control procedures
Watching the monthly bank reconciliation process
Observing credit approval procedures

assertions_tested.primarily_controls: Observation is primarily used for tests of controls to assess OPERATING effectiveness
assertions_tested.inventory_existence: Special case - observation of inventory count addresses existence assertion for inventory

strengths.operating_effectiveness: Confirms controls are actually performed as documented

limitations.point_in_time: Only provides evidence about WHEN the auditor is present, not the rest of the year
limitations.hawthorne_effect: People may perform differently when being observed
limitations.subsequent_performance: Doesn't prove controls operated effectively during unobserved periods

type_3_observation.exam_context: Observation is REQUIRED for inventory counts but must be SUPPLEMENTED with other procedures (tests of controls, subsequent testing) for year-round evidence.
type_3_observation.combining_procedures: Observation is often combined with inquiry and inspection. Example: Observe inventory count (observation), ask counter how to handle damaged items (inquiry), inspect count sheets (inspection).

type_4_external_confirmation.definition: Audit evidence obtained as a direct written response to the auditor from a third party (the confirming party) in paper, electronic, or other medium.
type_4_external_confirmation.reliability: VERY HIGH - one of the most reliable forms of evidence when obtained properly (sent by auditor, returned directly to auditor)
type_4_external_confirmation.exam_importance: CRITICAL - confirmation is heavily tested. Know the types, when required, and how to handle non-responses.

positive_confirmation.description: Requests that the recipient respond to the auditor in all cases, whether they agree or disagree with the information stated.
positive_confirmation.when_used: Higher risk situations, material balances, reason to believe recipients will respond
positive_confirmation.examples: Accounts receivable confirmations, bank confirmations, loan confirmations

response_types.blank_form: More reliable - asks recipient to fill in the balance (they must look it up)
response_types.invoice_form: Lists specific invoices, asks for confirmation
response_types.balance_form: States the balance, asks recipient to confirm or report differences

negative_confirmation.description: Requests recipient to respond ONLY if they disagree with the stated information.
negative_confirmation.reliability: LOWER than positive - no response could mean agreement OR that recipient ignored the request
negative_confirmation.when_allowed: Only when ALL of the following conditions are met: (1) RMM is LOW, (2) Large number of small balances, (3) Expect low exception rate, (4) Expect recipients will give requests adequate consideration
negative_confirmation.example: Confirming small customer accounts receivable balances when controls are strong

accounts_receivable.requirement: PRESUMPTIVELY MANDATORY - auditor should confirm A/R unless: (1) A/R is immaterial, (2) Confirmation would be ineffective, or (3) Combined RMM and detection risk is low and other procedures provide sufficient evidence
accounts_receivable.exam_note: A/R confirmation is the most tested confirmation topic

bank_confirmations.description: Standard bank confirmation obtains: deposit balances, loan balances, contingent liabilities, pledged assets
bank_confirmations.requirement: REQUIRED for all audits - must confirm all bank accounts

legal_confirmations.description: Attorney letter regarding litigation, claims, and assessments
legal_confirmations.requirement: REQUIRED - must inquire of client's attorneys
legal_confirmations.timing: As close to report date as practicable

common_confirmations.other_confirmations: Accounts payable, inventory held by third parties, investments held by custodians, debt agreements, insurance policies

confirmation_process.step_1: Auditor determines what to confirm and selects sample
confirmation_process.step_2: Client prepares confirmation requests on client letterhead
confirmation_process.step_3: AUDITOR MUST CONTROL the confirmation process - auditor reviews and mails confirmations
confirmation_process.step_4: Responses returned DIRECTLY to auditor (not to client - risk of interception)
confirmation_process.step_5: Auditor evaluates responses and performs alternative procedures for non-responses

nonresponses_and_alternative_procedures.issue: Not receiving a confirmation response is NOT audit evidence. The auditor must perform alternative procedures.
alternative_procedures_for_AR: Examine subsequent cash receipts (customer paid = account existed)
Inspect shipping documents and sales invoices
Examine sales orders and customer correspondence
nonresponses_and_alternative_procedures.exam_tip: Subsequent cash receipts is the MOST common alternative procedure for unconfirmed accounts receivable

assertions_addressed.existence_occurrence: STRONG - external party confirms the transaction or balance exists
assertions_addressed.rights_and_obligations: STRONG - bank confirms company owns the deposits
assertions_addressed.valuation: MODERATE - confirms amount but may not address collectibility or market value
assertions_addressed.completeness: WEAK - confirms what's on the list but not what's missing

type_4_external_confirmation.exam_strategy: When a question asks for the MOST reliable evidence, confirmation is often the correct answer (if available for that assertion).

type_5_recalculation.definition: Checking the mathematical accuracy of documents or records. The auditor independently performs calculations.
type_5_recalculation.reliability: VERY HIGH - when auditor recalculates, there's no subjectivity or client bias
examples: Recalculating depreciation expense
Recalculating interest expense on loans
Recalculating payroll tax withholdings
Footing and crossfooting spreadsheets and schedules
Recalculating inventory extensions (quantity × price)
Verifying mathematical accuracy of aged trial balance
Recalculating amortization of bond discount/premium
Recalculating earnings per share

assertions_tested.accuracy_valuation: PRIMARY - recalculation directly tests whether amounts are correctly calculated
assertions_tested.other_assertions: Generally not addressing existence, completeness, or rights - only whether the math is correct

type_5_recalculation.strengths: Provides definitive evidence about mathematical accuracy - no judgment required
type_5_recalculation.limitations: Only tests calculation, not underlying inputs. If you recalculate depreciation using wrong useful life, calculation is 'correct' but answer is wrong.
type_5_recalculation.exam_distinction: RECALCULATION is different from REPERFORMANCE - recalculation is just math; reperformance includes re-executing a control or substantive procedure.

type_6_reperformance.definition: The auditor's independent execution of procedures or controls that were originally performed by the client. Goes beyond recalculation to include re-doing the entire process.
type_6_reperformance.reliability: VERY HIGH - auditor performs the procedure independently
examples: Re-performing the bank reconciliation
Re-performing the aging of accounts receivable
Re-performing credit approval procedures
Re-performing matching of receiving reports to vendor invoices
Re-performing journal entry posting to general ledger
Re-performing the physical inventory count compilation
type_6_reperformance.assertions_tested: Depends on what's being reperformed - can address multiple assertions
type_6_reperformance.use_in_tests_of_controls: Reperformance is commonly used in tests of controls to verify controls are operating effectively. Example: Re-perform the three-way match (PO, receiving report, invoice) to verify the control works.
type_6_reperformance.comparison_to_inspection: REPERFORMANCE (auditor does it) provides more reliable evidence than INSPECTION (auditor looks at what client did)
type_6_reperformance.exam_tip: Reperformance provides highly reliable evidence but is time-consuming, so often used on a sample basis

type_7_analytical_procedures.definition: Evaluations of financial information made by studying plausible relationships among financial and non-financial data. Includes ratio analysis, trend analysis, and reasonableness testing.
type_7_analytical_procedures.reliability: VARIES - depends on precision of expectation, reliability of data used, and whether assertion is subject to estimation
type_7_analytical_procedures.exam_importance: Analytical procedures are REQUIRED in planning and final review. They're optional (but common) as substantive procedures.

types_of_analytical_procedures.trend_analysis: Comparing current year to prior years (revenue, expenses, ratios over time)
types_of_analytical_procedures.ratio_analysis: Computing and analyzing financial ratios (gross margin, current ratio, turnover ratios)
types_of_analytical_procedures.reasonableness_tests: Developing an independent expectation (units sold × average price = revenue)
types_of_analytical_procedures.relationship_analysis: Payroll expense should correlate with headcount; utilities with square footage

when_used.required_in_planning: Auditor MUST perform analytical procedures in planning to identify unusual relationships and areas of risk
when_used.optional_substantive: Can be used as substantive procedures to obtain evidence about assertions (often for income statement accounts)
when_used.required_final_review: Auditor MUST perform analytical procedures near the end of the audit to assess overall reasonableness

effectiveness_factors.precision: More precise expectations (detailed, specific) provide more persuasive evidence than vague expectations
effectiveness_factors.reliability_of_data: Procedures are more effective when based on reliable data (external sources, effective controls)
effectiveness_factors.predictability: More effective for predictable relationships (depreciation based on fixed assets) than unpredictable (legal fees)

examples_by_account.interest_expense: Calculate expected interest: Loan balance × interest rate. Compare to recorded interest expense.
examples_by_account.depreciation: Calculate expected depreciation: Fixed assets × depreciation rate. Compare to recorded depreciation.
examples_by_account.commission_expense: Calculate expected commissions: Sales × commission rate. Compare to recorded commissions.
examples_by_account.rental_income: Square footage × average rent per square foot × occupancy rate. Compare to recorded rental income.

assertions_addressed.completeness: Can be effective - if you expect $500K in interest based on debt outstanding but only $300K is recorded, may indicate completeness problem
assertions_addressed.occurrence_existence: Less effective - procedures may not detect fictitious transactions that appear reasonable
assertions_addressed.valuation: Moderately effective depending on precision of expectation

type_7_analytical_procedures.investigation_of_differences: When analytical procedures identify unexpected differences, the auditor must INVESTIGATE. Management explanations must be CORROBORATED with other evidence. This is where professional skepticism is critical.
type_7_analytical_procedures.exam_scenario: Question gives you data (e.g., average debt balance, interest rate) and asks you to develop an expectation for interest expense. You must calculate the expected amount and identify that recorded amount differs significantly.

combining_procedures.description: In practice, auditors rarely use just one type of evidence. Multiple procedures are combined to address assertions from different angles.
combining_procedures.rationale: Different procedures provide evidence about different assertions. Combining procedures provides more persuasive evidence than any single procedure.

example_accounts_receivable.objective: Obtain sufficient appropriate evidence about accounts receivable assertions
procedures_combined: CONFIRMATION - addresses existence and rights (external evidence, highly reliable)
INSPECTION of aged trial balance - addresses completeness and valuation (internal evidence)
ANALYTICAL PROCEDURES - compare receivable turnover to prior year and industry
INSPECTION of subsequent cash receipts - provides evidence about existence and valuation
RECALCULATION - foot the aged trial balance to verify mathematical accuracy
INQUIRY and inspection - ask about and examine documentation for old/unusual balances
example_accounts_receivable.why_combination_needed: Confirmation alone doesn't address valuation (collectibility). Analytical procedures alone don't provide account-level evidence. Combining procedures addresses all relevant assertions.

procedures_combined: OBSERVATION - observe physical inventory count (existence assertion)
INSPECTION - examine inventory for damage/obsolescence (valuation assertion)
ANALYTICAL PROCEDURES - analyze inventory turnover and gross margin (reasonableness)
CONFIRMATION - confirm inventory held by third parties (existence and rights)
INSPECTION of documents - examine purchase invoices for costs (valuation)

combining_procedures.professional_judgment: The auditor must use professional judgment to determine which combination of procedures will provide sufficient appropriate evidence based on the RMM for each assertion.

contradictory_evidence.description: Sometimes audit evidence from different sources or of a different nature may be contradictory. This requires careful evaluation.
contradictory_evidence.standard_requirement: If audit evidence obtained from one source is inconsistent with evidence obtained from another source, or if the auditor has doubts about the reliability of information to be used as audit evidence, the auditor must determine what modifications or additions to audit procedures are necessary to resolve the matter.

scenario_1.situation: Customer confirms $100,000 receivable balance, but subsequent cash receipts show only $60,000 received, with customer claiming the account is fully paid.
scenario_1.action_required: Investigate the discrepancy. Inspect supporting documentation (invoices, shipping documents, payment records). Determine if there's a dispute, error, or potential misstatement.
scenario_1.resolution: May discover timing differences, returns not recorded, or indication of fraudulent revenue recognition.

scenario_2.situation: Analytical procedures suggest inventory should be approximately $2 million based on turnover ratios, but recorded inventory is $3 million.
scenario_2.action_required: Investigate the unexpected difference. Perform additional procedures such as: review for obsolete inventory, test pricing, examine purchase cutoff, inquire with management.
scenario_2.importance: Cannot simply accept management's explanation without corroboration.

scenario_3.situation: Physical observation confirms equipment exists, but title search shows equipment is owned by leasing company.
scenario_3.action_required: Investigate the rights assertion. Review lease agreements, examine financial statement disclosures, determine if lease is properly classified.

contradictory_evidence.professional_skepticism: Contradictory evidence requires the auditor to apply heightened professional skepticism. Do not simply accept the evidence that supports management's position - investigate until the contradiction is resolved.
contradictory_evidence.documentation: The auditor must document how contradictory evidence was resolved and what additional procedures were performed.

insufficient_evidence.description: If the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, this is a scope limitation that affects the audit opinion.

causes.client_imposed: Management refuses to allow the auditor to confirm receivables, observe inventory, or obtain attorney letter
causes.circumstance_imposed: Auditor engaged after year-end and unable to observe inventory count; records destroyed in fire

impact_on_opinion.material_but_not_pervasive: QUALIFIED opinion ('except for' the scope limitation)
impact_on_opinion.material_and_pervasive: DISCLAIMER of opinion (unable to obtain sufficient evidence to form an opinion)

example_1.situation: Auditor engaged after year-end, unable to observe physical inventory count (material amount)
example_1.required_action: Perform alternative procedures: (1) Observe current inventory count and reconcile back, (2) Test intervening transactions (purchases, sales, production), (3) Review perpetual records, (4) Test shipping/receiving cutoff
example_1.outcome: If alternative procedures provide sufficient appropriate evidence, unmodified opinion possible. If not, qualified opinion or disclaimer.

example_2.situation: Management refuses to allow auditor to confirm accounts receivable (material amount)
example_2.required_action: Determine if alternative procedures can provide sufficient appropriate evidence: subsequent cash receipts, examination of shipping documents and sales invoices
example_2.outcome: If client-imposed scope limitation and alternatives insufficient, likely qualified or disclaimer (depending on pervasiveness).

insufficient_evidence.exam_tip: Inability to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence = scope limitation. Know the reporting implications.

professional_skepticism.description: Professional skepticism is an attitude that includes a questioning mind and critical assessment of audit evidence. It's fundamental to evidence evaluation.
professional_skepticism.definition_AU_C_200: Professional skepticism is an attitude that includes a questioning mind, being alert to conditions that may indicate possible misstatement due to fraud or error, and a critical assessment of audit evidence.

application_to_evidence.do_not_assume: Don't assume management is honest or dishonest - evaluate evidence objectively
application_to_evidence.corroborate_explanations: When management provides an explanation for unusual items, CORROBORATE with evidence. Don't simply accept oral representations.
application_to_evidence.question_contradictory_evidence: When evidence conflicts, investigate rather than choosing the evidence that's easier to obtain or supports a desired conclusion
application_to_evidence.consider_reliability: Critically assess the source and reliability of evidence - is it from an independent source? Could it be biased?

professional_skepticism.fraud_considerations: Professional skepticism is especially important when fraud risk factors are present. The auditor should not be satisfied with less-than-persuasive evidence when fraud risks exist.

examples.example_1: Management explains that revenue increased 50% due to 'improved marketing.' Professional skepticism requires the auditor to corroborate this with evidence: examine marketing campaigns, analyze customer mix, test revenue transactions, review for side agreements.
examples.example_2: Controller provides detailed analysis of inventory obsolescence reserve. Professional skepticism requires auditor to verify assumptions, test underlying data, inspect slow-moving inventory, not just accept the analysis.
examples.example_3: CFO explains unexpected analytical procedure result as 'timing difference.' Professional skepticism requires verification of the timing difference with evidence, not acceptance of oral explanation.

professional_skepticism.exam_context: Questions often present a scenario where management provides an explanation. The correct answer typically involves CORROBORATING the explanation with additional procedures rather than accepting it.

relationship_to_assertions.description: Different types of evidence are more effective for different assertions. Understanding which procedures best address which assertions is critical.

existence_occurrence.best_procedures: Confirmation, observation, inspection of tangible assets
existence_occurrence.why: These provide direct evidence that transactions occurred or assets exist
existence_occurrence.example: Confirming accounts receivable directly addresses existence

completeness.best_procedures: Analytical procedures, tracing from source documents to accounting records, inspection of subsequent transactions
completeness.why: Need to look for what might be MISSING - harder to prove than existence
completeness.example: Analytical procedures showing lower-than-expected payables may indicate missing liabilities
completeness.challenge: Most difficult assertion to test - can't examine what isn't recorded

rights_and_obligations.best_procedures: Confirmation, inspection of contracts and agreements, inspection of title documents
rights_and_obligations.why: Need legal evidence of ownership or obligations
rights_and_obligations.example: Inspecting title documents for property or confirming with bank that assets aren't pledged

valuation_accuracy.best_procedures: Recalculation, inspection of supporting documents, analytical procedures, confirmation
valuation_accuracy.why: Need to verify amounts are correct
valuation_accuracy.example: Recalculating depreciation or inspecting vendor invoices to verify inventory costs

presentation_disclosure.best_procedures: Inspection of contracts and agreements, reading financial statements, inquiry with management and legal counsel
presentation_disclosure.why: Need to verify proper classification and adequate disclosure
presentation_disclosure.example: Inspecting lease agreements to determine proper classification as operating vs. finance lease

relationship_to_audit_risk.description: The nature, timing, and extent of evidence gathering is directly related to the assessed risk of material misstatement.

higher_risk_more_evidence.quality: Higher RMM requires MORE RELIABLE evidence (appropriateness)
higher_risk_more_evidence.nature: May need to shift from less reliable to more reliable procedures (from inspection to confirmation)
higher_risk_more_evidence.timing: May need to test closer to year-end rather than interim

example.scenario: Revenue has fraud risk factors (management incentive, pressure to meet targets)
example.response: Perform MORE substantive procedures, use MORE reliable evidence (confirmation rather than inspection), test closer to year-end, increase sample sizes, apply heightened skepticism

relationship_to_materiality.description: Materiality affects both the amount of evidence needed and the nature of procedures performed.
relationship_to_materiality.more_material_more_evidence: More material items require more extensive testing and more persuasive evidence
relationship_to_materiality.example: A $50 million customer receivable requires more evidence (confirmation, subsequent cash receipts, credit analysis) than a $5,000 receivable

electronic_evidence.description: Modern audits increasingly involve electronic evidence, which presents unique considerations.

characteristics.ease_of_alteration: Electronic evidence can be altered without trace if controls are weak
characteristics.dependency_on_IT_controls: Reliability depends heavily on IT general controls and application controls
characteristics.availability: May only exist electronically - no paper trail

auditor_considerations.IT_controls_assessment: Must evaluate IT general controls (access, change management, backups) to determine reliability
auditor_considerations.data_analytics: Electronic data enables powerful analytical procedures and detailed transaction testing
auditor_considerations.specialized_skills: May require IT audit specialists for complex systems

electronic_evidence.example: System-generated sales reports are reliable evidence if IT general controls are effective. If controls are weak (poor access controls, inadequate change management), the auditor places less reliance on system reports and performs more manual testing.

practice_problems.question:
An auditor is testing accounts receivable and considers the following procedures:

Procedure A: Examining the accounts receivable aged trial balance prepared by the client
Procedure B: Confirming accounts receivable balances directly with customers, with responses sent directly to the auditor
Procedure C: Examining subsequent cash receipts from customers
Procedure D: Inquiring with management about the collectibility of receivables

Required:
1. Rank these procedures from MOST to LEAST reliable
2. Explain which assertion each procedure primarily addresses
3. If the client has weak internal controls over accounts receivable, how would this affect your reliance on each procedure?

part_1_ranking.most_reliable: Procedure B - Confirmation (external evidence obtained directly by auditor)
part_1_ranking.second: Procedure C - Subsequent cash receipts (external evidence - customer actually paid)
part_1_ranking.third: Procedure A - Aged trial balance (internal evidence from client)
part_1_ranking.least_reliable: Procedure D - Management inquiry (oral representation, least reliable)

part_2_assertions.procedure_A: Completeness and valuation - the aging shows all receivables and categorizes by age for allowance assessment
part_2_assertions.procedure_B: Existence and rights - confirmation proves the receivable exists and the customer acknowledges owing it
part_2_assertions.procedure_C: Existence and valuation - if customer paid, receivable existed and was collectible
part_2_assertions.procedure_D: Valuation - management's assessment of collectibility, but must be corroborated

part_3_weak_controls.procedure_A: SIGNIFICANTLY LESS reliable - cannot trust client-prepared aging if controls are weak. Would need to test accuracy extensively.
part_3_weak_controls.procedure_B: UNCHANGED reliability - still highly reliable external evidence regardless of client controls
part_3_weak_controls.procedure_C: UNCHANGED reliability - still reliable external evidence (bank records show payment)
part_3_weak_controls.procedure_D: LESS reliable - if controls are weak, management may not have accurate information about collectibility

solution.key_takeaway: External evidence (B and C) maintains reliability regardless of control environment. Internal evidence (A and D) becomes less reliable when controls are weak. The auditor should shift toward more external evidence when controls are weak.

practice_problems.question:
An auditor is planning substantive procedures for inventory and is considering the following:

Scenario: The client has inventory valued at $5 million (material). The auditor observes the physical inventory count at year-end and notes the following:
- Count appears accurate
- Some inventory appears dusty and slow-moving
- Client uses FIFO cost method
- Inventory turnover ratio has decreased from 8x to 4x

Required:
1. Which assertion(s) does physical observation of inventory primarily address?
2. Which assertion(s) are NOT adequately addressed by observation alone?
3. What additional procedures should the auditor perform and why?
4. How do the decreased turnover and slow-moving appearance affect the audit approach?

part_1_observation_addresses.existence: PRIMARY assertion - observation confirms inventory physically exists
part_1_observation_addresses.note: Observation is the most direct and persuasive evidence for inventory existence

part_2_not_addressed.valuation: NOT addressed - seeing inventory doesn't prove it's worth the recorded amount. Could be obsolete, damaged, or overvalued.
part_2_not_addressed.rights_and_obligations: NOT fully addressed - observation shows possession but doesn't prove ownership (could be consignment inventory or customer-owned goods)
part_2_not_addressed.completeness: NOT addressed - can't see inventory that should be there but isn't
part_2_not_addressed.presentation: NOT addressed - observation doesn't determine proper classification

part_3_additional_procedures.why: Verify cost by examining vendor invoices - addresses valuation
The dusty, slow-moving inventory and decreased turnover suggest potential obsolescence. Compare costs to net realizable value, review sales prices, inquire about slow-moving items.
Decreased turnover indicates inventory is older - need to assess obsolescence risk

part_3_additional_procedures.procedure: Confirm inventory held by third parties or consignment inventory
part_3_additional_procedures.why: Ensure inventory recorded is owned and inventory not recorded (consignment out) is excluded
Ensure inventory purchased/sold near year-end is recorded in correct period
Verify mathematical accuracy of FIFO calculations
Analyze gross margin and turnover trends to identify unusual relationships suggesting valuation issues

part_4_risk_assessment.valuation_risk: INCREASED RISK - decreased turnover and slow-moving appearance suggest higher risk of overvaluation due to obsolescence
part_4_risk_assessment.impact_on_procedures: Need MORE evidence about valuation - expand testing of obsolescence, NRV, pricing. May need to lower performance materiality for inventory.
part_4_risk_assessment.professional_skepticism: Apply heightened skepticism to management's obsolescence reserve. Don't simply accept their calculation - verify assumptions, test underlying data, physically inspect slow-moving items.

solution.key_exam_point: Observation addresses EXISTENCE but NOT valuation. Additional procedures are ALWAYS needed for inventory. Decreased turnover is a RED FLAG for obsolescence.

practice_problems.question:
During an audit, the following situations occur:

Situation 1: The auditor sends confirmations to 100 customers for accounts receivable ($5 million total). 60 customers respond confirming balances, 40 do not respond.

Situation 2: The auditor performs analytical procedures and calculates expected interest expense should be $400,000 based on average debt outstanding and stated interest rates. Recorded interest expense is $280,000. Management explains the difference is due to 'debt being paid off mid-year.'

Situation 3: The auditor observes equipment that is recorded on the fixed asset register at $200,000. A title search reveals the equipment is owned by a leasing company.

Required:
For each situation:
1. Identify the issue
2. Describe what additional procedures the auditor must perform
3. Explain the potential audit and financial statement implications

situation_1_nonresponses.issue: 40% non-response rate - non-responses are NOT audit evidence. Cannot conclude anything from lack of response.
additional_procedures: PRIMARY: Examine subsequent cash receipts from non-responding customers (if customer paid, receivable existed)
Examine sales invoices and shipping documents for non-responding customers
Examine sales orders and customer correspondence
Consider sending second requests to non-responding customers
situation_1_nonresponses.determination: Evaluate if alternative procedures provide sufficient appropriate evidence. If not, may be a scope limitation.
situation_1_nonresponses.assertion_addressed: Alternative procedures should address existence assertion (what confirmation would have addressed)
situation_1_nonresponses.exam_note: Subsequent cash receipts is the MOST COMMON and MOST EFFECTIVE alternative procedure for unconfirmed receivables.

situation_2_analytical_difference.issue: Significant unexplained difference ($120,000 or 30% difference) between expected and recorded interest expense. Management explanation must be CORROBORATED - cannot simply accept oral explanation.
additional_procedures: Examine debt agreements and payment schedules to verify timing of debt payoff
Recalculate interest expense based on actual debt balances and dates
Trace debt payments to bank statements and cash disbursements
Confirm outstanding debt balances with lenders (standard bank confirmation)
Review board minutes for approval of debt payoff
Examine use of proceeds to verify debt was paid (not embezzled)
potential_implications: BEST CASE: Management explanation is correct - debt was paid off mid-year, interest calculation was correct
CONCERN: Interest expense is understated (completeness issue) - missing accrual or calculation error
FRAUD RISK: Misappropriation of assets - 'debt payoff' was actually funds misappropriated, interest not recorded to hide the theft
situation_2_analytical_difference.professional_skepticism: This situation requires heightened skepticism. Unexplained differences in predictable accounts (interest is highly predictable) are RED FLAGS. Do not accept management's explanation without thorough verification.
situation_2_analytical_difference.exam_principle: Analytical procedures that reveal unexpected differences require INVESTIGATION and CORROBORATION. Oral management explanations are insufficient.

situation_3_contradictory_evidence.issue: Contradictory evidence - observation shows possession (existence) but title search shows lack of ownership (rights). This is a RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS assertion problem.
additional_procedures: Examine lease agreement to determine nature of lease
Determine if lease should be classified as operating or finance lease under ASC 842
If finance lease: verify right-of-use asset and lease liability are properly recorded
If operating lease: verify equipment is REMOVED from fixed asset register and lease is properly disclosed
Recalculate lease accounting (present value, amortization, interest)
Review other fixed assets for similar situations (systematic problem?)
Inquire with management why equipment is on fixed asset register
potential_financial_statement_implicatio: MISCLASSIFICATION: Operating lease improperly recorded as owned asset
UNDERSTATEMENT: If finance lease, lease liability understated
DISCLOSURE: Lease disclosures may be inadequate or incorrect
FRAUD CONSIDERATION: Intentional misclassification to improve balance sheet appearance?
situation_3_contradictory_evidence.impact_on_opinion: If material and not corrected, likely QUALIFIED opinion for departure from GAAP (improper classification of lease)
situation_3_contradictory_evidence.exam_principle: Physical observation addresses EXISTENCE but not RIGHTS. Title documents or confirmations are needed for rights assertion. Contradictory evidence MUST be resolved - cannot ignore one set of evidence.

tip_1_hierarchy_questions.description: Many exam questions ask which procedure provides the MOST reliable or MOST persuasive evidence.
tip_1_hierarchy_questions.strategy: Apply the reliability hierarchy: External > Auditor-generated > Internal. Within external, direct to auditor > indirect. Within procedures, confirmation > observation > inspection.
tip_1_hierarchy_questions.example: Question: Which provides the MOST persuasive evidence about accounts receivable existence? Options: (A) Client-prepared aging, (B) Subsequent cash receipts, (C) Customer confirmation, (D) Management inquiry. Answer: (C) - external evidence obtained directly by auditor.

tip_2_assertion_matching.description: Questions often describe a procedure and ask which assertion is addressed.
tip_2_assertion_matching.strategy: Know what each procedure does and doesn't address. Observation = existence, NOT valuation. Confirmation = existence and rights, WEAK for completeness.
tip_2_assertion_matching.common_trap: Thinking observation of inventory addresses valuation - it doesn't. Observation only addresses existence.

tip_3_sufficiency_vs_appropriateness.description: Questions may describe evidence and ask if it's sufficient or appropriate.
tip_3_sufficiency_vs_appropriateness.strategy: Appropriate = quality (is it relevant and reliable?). Sufficient = quantity (is there enough?). Can have appropriate evidence that isn't sufficient (need more). Cannot compensate for inappropriate evidence with quantity.
tip_3_sufficiency_vs_appropriateness.example: 100 unconfirmed receivables are LESS persuasive than 50 confirmed receivables - quantity doesn't overcome quality.

tip_4_confirmation_questions.description: Confirmations are heavily tested - know types, when required, alternative procedures.
key_facts: Positive confirmation is more reliable than negative
Blank form positive is more reliable than balance form
Non-responses require alternative procedures - subsequent cash receipts is most common
Negative confirmation only allowed when RMM is low, many small balances, low exception rate expected

tip_5_management_representations.description: Management representations are REQUIRED but are the LEAST reliable evidence.
tip_5_management_representations.key_point: Oral or written representations must be CORROBORATED with other procedures. Never sufficient on their own.
tip_5_management_representations.exam_scenario: Question describes auditor obtaining management representation. Answer will likely require ADDITIONAL procedures to corroborate.

tip_6_contradictory_evidence.description: Questions may present contradictory evidence and ask what the auditor should do.
tip_6_contradictory_evidence.correct_approach: INVESTIGATE and perform additional procedures. Do not ignore one set of evidence. Do not simply accept management's explanation.
tip_6_contradictory_evidence.wrong_approach: Accepting the evidence that's easier or that supports management's position.

tip_7_analytical_procedures.description: Know when analytical procedures are required vs. optional.
tip_7_analytical_procedures.required: Planning (risk assessment) and final review (overall reasonableness)
tip_7_analytical_procedures.optional: As substantive procedures (but commonly used for income statement accounts)
tip_7_analytical_procedures.effectiveness: More effective for predictable accounts (interest, depreciation) than unpredictable (legal fees, repairs)

tip_8_observation_vs_inspection.observation: Watching a PROCESS being performed (inventory count, opening mail)
tip_8_observation_vs_inspection.inspection: Examining RECORDS, DOCUMENTS, or TANGIBLE ASSETS (invoices, equipment)
tip_8_observation_vs_inspection.exam_trap: Observation of inventory count vs. inspection of inventory - different procedures

tip_9_recalculation_vs_reperformance.recalculation: Checking the MATH only (footing, depreciation calculation)
tip_9_recalculation_vs_reperformance.reperformance: Re-executing the entire PROCEDURE (re-performing bank reconciliation, re-aging A/R)
tip_9_recalculation_vs_reperformance.reliability: Both highly reliable - auditor performs independently

tip_10_completeness_assertion.description: Completeness is the hardest assertion to test - you're looking for what's MISSING.
tip_10_completeness_assertion.best_procedures: Analytical procedures (expected vs. actual), tracing from source documents forward, testing subsequent transactions
tip_10_completeness_assertion.example: To test completeness of accounts payable, examine RECEIVING reports and trace to recorded payables (not the reverse - that tests existence)

common_exam_question_types.type: Which procedure provides the MOST reliable evidence?
common_exam_question_types.approach: Apply reliability hierarchy - external, auditor-generated wins
Match procedure to assertion - observation=existence, confirmation=existence/rights, analytical=completeness/valuation

common_exam_question_types.type: What should the auditor do when [contradictory evidence]?
common_exam_question_types.approach: Investigate and perform additional procedures - never ignore contradictory evidence
Subsequent cash receipts is primary alternative

common_exam_question_types.type: Calculate expected amount using analytical procedures
common_exam_question_types.approach: Use given data (interest rate × loan balance = expected interest) and compare to recorded amount

memorization_aids.seven_types_of_evidence_mnemonic: I CARE: Inspection (records), Confirmation, Analytical, Recalculation, External confirmation, + Observation, Reperformance (ICAROR - harder to remember, just memorize all 7)
memorization_aids.reliability_hierarchy_simple: External > Auditor > Internal; Direct > Indirect; Written > Oral; Original > Copy
memorization_aids.assertions_mnemonic: CEAVOP: Completeness, Existence/Occurrence, Accuracy/Valuation, Rights/Obligations, Presentation/Disclosure
memorization_aids.confirmation_types: Positive = always respond. Negative = only if disagree. Blank = most reliable (must look it up).

key_concepts: Audit evidence must be BOTH sufficient (quantity) and appropriate (quality) - dual requirement
Evidence reliability hierarchy: External > Auditor-generated > Internal; Direct > Indirect; Written > Oral
Seven types of evidence: Inspection (records and tangible assets), Observation, Confirmation, Recalculation, Reperformance, Analytical procedures
Different procedures address different assertions - must match procedure to assertion being tested
Confirmation is presumptively mandatory for A/R and required for banks
Non-responses to confirmations require alternative procedures (subsequent cash receipts primary)
Management representations are required but least reliable - must corroborate
Contradictory or insufficient evidence requires investigation and additional procedures
Professional skepticism requires critical assessment and corroboration of management explanations
Higher RMM requires more and better evidence; more material items require more evidence
critical_for_exam: Know the reliability hierarchy cold - external, auditor-generated, internal
Match procedures to assertions - observation=existence, NOT valuation
Confirmation rules - when required, types, alternative procedures
Analytical procedures required in planning and final review
Completeness is hardest assertion to test
common_mistakes_to_avoid: Thinking observation addresses valuation - it doesn't, only existence
Believing quantity of evidence compensates for poor quality - it doesn't
Confusing observation (watching process) with inspection (examining records/assets)
Thinking non-responses to confirmations are evidence - they're not, need alternatives

primary_standards: AU-C Section 500: Audit Evidence - defines sufficient appropriate evidence, types of procedures, reliability factors
AU-C Section 505: External Confirmations - confirmation requirements, types, alternative procedures
AU-C Section 520: Analytical Procedures - when required, effectiveness factors, investigation of differences
AU-C Section 200: Overall Objectives - defines professional skepticism
related_standards: AU-C Section 501: Audit Evidence—Specific Considerations for Selected Items (inventory, litigation, segment information)
AU-C Section 230: Audit Documentation - documentation of evidence obtained
AU-C Section 330: Performing Audit Procedures in Response to Assessed Risks - designing procedures based on risk

related_topics: audit_risk_model - evidence gathering is driven by assessed RMM
audit_planning_procedures - evidence needs are planned during planning phase
internal_control_testing - tests of controls provide evidence about control effectiveness
substantive_testing - substantive procedures gather evidence about assertions
audit_sampling - sampling determines how much evidence to examine
audit_documentation - evidence must be documented in workpapers
audit_reports_opinions - evidence supports the opinion; insufficient evidence = scope limitation
